messages.subject: Bayes Factors via product spaces?
messages.body_plain:
I was not able to definitively answer Martin Smira's question
about whether it would be possible to implement the product-space
approach to Bayes factor computations with HMC.

This was developed by Carlin and Chib:

  B.P. Carlin, S. Chib
  Bayesian model choice via Markov chain Monte Carlo methods
  Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 57 (1995), pp. 473–484

There's also an overview in a (paywalled) psych journal that kicked
off the discussion (Lee and Wagenmakers are two of the co-authors):

  http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022249611000423

And there's a discussion by Charles Geyer in the umbrella sampling chapter of
the MCMC Handbook (not one of the free chapters, I'm afraid).

The most explicit reference I saw for how a model like this can be
coded is in a BUGS vol2 example:

  http://www.medicine.mcgill.ca/epidemiology/joseph/courses/EPIB-682/pines.pdf

We do not have that example working in Stan, nor could I get a version
working.  From what I can tell, the product-space approach simulates a reversible
jump MCMC method with Gibbs sampling and pseudo-priors, with some fiddly
pre-tuning required to adjust the pseudo-priors.  But I'm afraid I don't even
understand why it'd work in BUGS because the posterior just looks wrong (so there's
probably something I'm not understanding --- like maybe they only take the parameter
samples from one of the branches [which clearly won't work in Stan]).

I had problems trying to conceptualize what the model would even look
like in Stan and was wondering if anyone had any suggestions or an explanation
of why it wouldn't be possible.

- Bob

messages.subject: mixture syntax
messages.body_plain:
Rob and I are going to tackle feature

  add mixture support functions
  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/970

as an example of how to code functions with autodiff.

*** QUESTION ***:  what should the function be called?

The feature request proposes two functions:

  1. binary mixture

  mix(real lambda, real lp1, real lp2)
    = log_sum_exp(log(lambda) + lp1, log1m(lambda) + lp2)

  where lambda must be in (0,1).

and

  2. general mixture

  mix(vector theta, vector lp)
    = log_sum_exp(log(theta) + lp)

  where theta is a K-simplex and lp a K-vector.

This would let us write a normal 2-mixture as:

  increment_log_prob(mix(lambda,
                         normal_log(y[n], mu[1], sigma[1]),
                         normal_log(y[n], mu[2], sigma[2])));

instead of what we have now:

  increment_log_prob(
    log_sum_exp(log(lambda) + normal_log(y[n], mu[1], sigma[1]),
                log1m(lambda) + normal_log(y[n], mu[2], sigma[2])));

and it'll reduce memory and speed up gradients.

If we call the function mix_log, we could even write:

  lambda ~ mix(normal_log(y[n], mu[1], sigma[1]),
               normal_log(y[n], mu[2], sigma[2])));

but that seems a bit weird, because it'd be super-confusing to
write the whole thing out as

  for (n in 1:N)
    lambda ~ mix(normal_log(y[n], mu[1], sigma[1]),
                 normal_log(y[n], mu[2], sigma[2])));

even though it'd do the right thing with the log prob accumulator
and is a less verbose syntax than

  for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(mix_log(lambda,
                               normal_log(y[n], mu[1], sigma[1]),
                               normal_log(y[n], mu[2], sigma[2])));

What I'd like to have eventually is something vectorized like this:

  y ~ finite_mixture<normal>(lambda, mu, sigma);

or some other syntax with a function-like argument "normal" that'd
expand to the above.  This would be a bit tricky on the syntactic side
to get everything to line up, but certainly possible.  It'd yield a new
kind of statement (or looked at from a user perspective, a new kind of
way for writing distributions down).

Or if we're going away from the sampling statement syntax, something
like:

  increment_log_prob(finite_mixture<normal>(y, lambda, mu, sigma));

Then finite_mixture... is a special kind of expression.

Maybe we should just drop the "increment_"?  And maybe capitalize?

  LOG_PROB(finite_mixture<normal>(y, lambda, mu, sigma));

It'd then just be read as marking erms in the overall log probabilty function.

- Bob

What I discovered when I started glmer2stan was that lme4's use of the parentheses for varying effects is idiosyncratic. Other and older packages, like lme and MCMCglmm, use separate formulas for fixed and varying effects. So lme4 does its own parsing into separate formulas, and then it passes formulas to the internal methods model.matrix (and model.frame I think) for processing. But it has to split apart the formulas first.

My parser does the same thing, but uses it's own parsed representation. You'll see in my github code that there are internal function nobars() and findbars() that recursively crawl through the tree structure of the formulas (R formulas are really function call trees) to do the splitting. Those are lme4 functions, for the most part. As much as I enjoy recursion, in hindsight it would probably be easier to convert the whole formula to text and use grep to do the splitting.

Bob's suggestion #2 sounds ambitious and very useful. Would be fantastic for CmdStan to have a linear formula parser.

> On Nov 13, 2014, at 9:20 AM, Richard McElreath <rmcel...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> What I discovered when I started glmer2stan was that lme4's use of the parentheses for varying effects is idiosyncratic. Other and older packages, like lme and MCMCglmm, use separate formulas for fixed and varying effects. So lme4 does its own parsing into separate formulas, and then it passes formulas to the internal methods model.matrix (and model.frame I think) for processing. But it has to split apart the formulas first.
>
> My parser does the same thing, but uses it's own parsed representation. You'll see in my github code that there are internal function nobars() and findbars() that recursively crawl through the tree structure of the formulas (R formulas are really function call trees) to do the splitting. Those are lme4 functions, for the most part. As much as I enjoy recursion, in hindsight it would probably be easier to convert the whole formula to text and use grep to do the splitting.
>
> Bob's suggestion #2 sounds ambitious and very useful. Would be fantastic for CmdStan to have a linear formula parser.

I don't want to let ambitious long-term plans get in the way
of our doing something reasonable for RStan in the short term.

Thanks much for the rundown on lme4 parsing.  I wonder
if JAGS does the same thing?

One reason we were considering writing our own parser is that
might want to extend the language somehow, particularly to allow
the representation of the models in Gelman and Hill's book which
can't be expressed in the lme4 language.

As to matrices, consider something like the simplest model.  It's
basically an (M + N) dimensional regression where there are M
students and N questions.  But only two of the dimensions are
ever on for any example, so coding this using matrix multiplication
would be really costly in Stan (we don't have a good way to optimize
out all the zeros, so they all get autodiffed).

As for extensions, if you consider the standard 2PL version of IRT,
you get another N parameters, but it's no longer a simple linear
model, so I think you're beyond what lme4 can do.  There's also
the identifiability issue.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Marking header functions as inline
messages.body_plain:
Well, if you look at the functions in the mentioned file, you'll see that they're basic, non-templated functions.  E.G., consider a foo.hpp which has:

void foo(double x, double y) {
...
}

if there are two cpp files that include foo.hpp, say a.cpp and b.cpp that get compiled separately and linked together:

g++ -c -o a.o a.cpp
g++ -c -o b.o b.cpp
g++ -o runme a.o b.o

Then the final compilation to runme will produce an error because the symbol foo was compiled and produced a symbol in both a.o and b.o and these conflict when they're linked together.

The solution (which keeps Stan mostly header-only) is to mark foo() as inline so the compiler doesn't generate a symbol for it in a.o and b.o.  You can also remove the definition of foo from the header and put it into a cpp file of it's own which is compiled separately and linked, but this would complicate model building and would do practically nothing for our compile times since these functions are (as far as I can tell) a very small part of the code base.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: knitr example and discussion
messages.body_plain:
I'm attaching my first knitr doc, which I rendered to
pdf from HTML because the HTML didn't seem to be robust
(more below).  It explains how to fit soil carbon model
parameters for a simple two-compartment model with feedback
based on data from a controlled soil incubation experiment.
Hopefully I included enough of a brief of the science that
it's understandable.  Any and all feedback on the models
welcome.  This one's the industry standard model, so I wanted to
fit that first.  Michael's already suggested going to a lognormal
noise to respect positivity constraints on concentrations, and that works
well.  I also implemented a measurement error model a la 8 schools,
because the actual data is made up of sample means and standard
deviations from replicated experiments.

I got the hard sell on knitr from David LeBauer (cc-ed) when I was out
in Arizona (David --- if you want to respond, I can forward to our
developers group if you'd like; feel free to forward elsewhere), based on:

  * reproducible science
  * literate programming
  * easier to learn than LaTeX

If you don't know what knitr is, it lets you write R "markdown"
(very similar to GitHub flavored "markdown") to generate either
an HTML or LaTeX (or even MSWord) document.  The document generation
process is called "knitting" (should be "knittering").  And like
knitting, it's awfully slow, even compared to running pdflatex
multiple times as we do for our manual with indexes and cross-refs and
bibs.

The reproducibility is tantalizing.  You can create an entire
sequence of operations and be sure that they run to produce the
right result.  For that reason, I thought it might be a good way
to present our examples.  Or write a textbook.  We'd then have the
Stan code, R code, and doc all together and they'd be guaranteed
to be in synch.  This is the big selling point for me.

I've been using LaTeX since 1984 (30 years!), so that's not an obstacle
for me.  Rather, I like is that it lets you embed LaTeX!

knitr is NOT like IPython notebooks in that a person looking at the knitted
document can't change some of the params and rerun it.  You have to download
the source, edit that, and then reknit the whole thing from scratch.
This wouldn't be a dealbreaker for my intended application to Stan examples, though,
and I went in knowing the score.

The major selling points of knitr are that

  * if you include the right escapes around R code (and apparently
    many other types), it will execute and the results will be dumped
    into the output document, including figures, and

  * if you use $...$, the formula making up the ellipses is converted
    to MathJAX and used to render on the client side.

Rendering MathJAX on the client side is slow.  I'm already tired of
watching Safari tell me how much progress I've made through it, and this
is only a small doc.

I'm not a big fan of "literate programming" if that means
mixing doc and code like this:

  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literate_programming

It's convenient for small projects, but I don't see how it's going to scale.
It also makes it hard to edit the code as it's all in one big honking editor
in RStudio.  Of course, I could edit the knitr source (format .Rmd for R markdown)
in emacs and then knit it from the command line using a script.  There seem to
be some robustness issues with editing while knitting, but I'm not sure that
wasn't some other problem I fat fingered on the interface.

Mixing text and code isn't so pretty.  I like my syntax highlighting and
I like to be able to see all the code I'm I'm working on at once without scrolling
around finding it interspersed with a textual exegesis.  I favor modularity over
automatic gathering.  I also like using one tool for everything.  To pull our
a cooking example, I'm a chef's knife and simple stainless steel pan kind of guy,
not a gadget guy.

I like managing all of my code separately and using my favorite editor to edit
it and my favorite tools to run it, like make.  It's a pain to get started that
way compared to just popping open a new markdown project in RStudio, but I think
the up front time is more than made up by everything then being easier downstream.

So I think I might like knitr better used outside of RStudio with
more use of includes and less of writing into a single document.
I had to write a little R script program just to dump unformatted code
into the document. There's probably a more elegant way, but I couldn't
find it.

I do not at all like the code editor or the R Markdown editor in RStudio.
I do appreciate the pop-up auto-complete and open global environment browser, given
how much R programming idioms (and even packages) lean on the global environment.
(And kudos to Jeffrey Arnold for getting that working in Stan's emacs mode, which
I love!)

I'm worried about applications of knitr to Stan because I couldn't figure out
how to get knitr's make-like behavior to cache the Stan fit object so that it
doesn't need to run each time.  Might it be because there's an outside file referenced
in it?  I can't bring myself to write my Stan program as a string embedded
in R code, but maybe that would work.

After two days, I'm not sold on RStudio (but then I came in with a very
anti-IDE prejudice).  As to RStudio:

  * It's unstable and not only crashed, but crashed my
    whole OS (I'm also not a huge fan of Mac OS X "Yosemite").

    Maybe that's what Andrew's problem has been!  Avi Feller was saying
    that RStan crashed in RStudio (not sure what hardware/OS), but never
    when run from the command line under Linux on a cluster.

  * RStudio gobbles some output, which I really don't like. Maybe
    that's configurable?

  * Like every other IDE, RStudio hides things and tries to be
    clever by automatically foregrounding and backgrounding
    windows and what not.  To change metaphors to the automotive
    industry (I am from Detroit), I prefer to shift myself because
    I haven't met an auto transmission that does it better (I hear
    they exist now --- I'm a New Yorker now and don't own a car and
    only rent crap cars like the Chevy Malibu I had in Arizona.)

Also, what's with all these R package docs?  I found the knitr
doc and web site, as it is, pretty much impenetrable.

  http://yihui.name/knitr/

In that way, it's just like ggplot2 (another RStudio gig), meaning
that I had to go to third-person resources to figure it out.  Good thing
there are so many great R tutorials out there!

Markdown.  I really hate working in markdown.  This goes for
WordPress, which uses WordPress markdown, and GitHub Wiki and issues,
which use GitHub "flavored" markdown.  I'd rather just write the HTML since
I'm going to have to figure out how it renders the HTML anyway
if I want a reasonable output.

The rendering of HTML and LaTeX is not seamless.  I wound up having to
write a gazillion straight-up HTML elements and styles to do things like float and
size pictures or to include captions.  That's an example of what I mean when I
say these markdown languages make easy things easier and hard things harder.

As a result, not everything shows up in LaTeX.   You can also write
in pseudo-LaTeX and have things rendered to HTML with the opposite
problem.  Or you can take a least-common denominator approach and get
ill-formatted docs both ways, but at least they'll be the same.

What's up with those awful knitr style sheets?  They violate standard
rules of typesetting like making headers closer to the text they
head than the text they follow.  Are there better ones somewhere
someone could recommend?  I do like that you can drop in your own stylesheet.
Then you just need to learn what knitr renders in the way of HTML
(just kidding --- this is why I don't like "clever" tools getting in
the way of my code;  if I wrote straight up HTML this issue goes away).

I sent my completely knitted doc to Rob, and he couldn't render
it on his machine.  Things seem to be messed up in both fonts and in
content.  Maybe the former is due to missing a char encoding declaration.
Odd, because it makes a 3MB web page that has everything inside it as data.
You'd think they'd control the fonts.  Now why you get what look like stub
captions when Rob renders it, I don't know.

At some point in Arizona, someone (maybe David) mentioned that they liked
that you don't have to paginate knitr output.  That does seem like a plus for
code and its output.

- Bob

...

or the timestamp of the file
```{r,cache.extra = file.mtime("foo.stan")}
...
```

> Stan code, R code, and doc all together and they'd be guaranteed
> to be in synch.  This is the big selling point for me.
>
> I've been using LaTeX since 1984 (30 years!), so that's not an obstacle
> for me.  Rather, I like is that it lets you embed LaTeX!
>
> knitr is NOT like IPython notebooks in that a person looking at the knitted
> document can't change some of the params and rerun it.  You have to download
> the source, edit that, and then reknit the whole thing from scratch.
> This wouldn't be a dealbreaker for my intended application to Stan examples, though,
> and I went in knowing the score.
>
> The major selling points of knitr are that
>
>   * if you include the right escapes around R code (and apparently
>     many other types), it will execute and the results will be dumped
>     into the output document, including figures, and
>
>   * if you use $...$, the formula making up the ellipses is converted
>     to MathJAX and used to render on the client side.
>
> Rendering MathJAX on the client side is slow.  I'm already tired of
> watching Safari tell me how much progress I've made through it, and this
> is only a small doc.
>
> I'm not a big fan of "literate programming" if that means
> mixing doc and code like this:
>
>   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literate_programming
>
> It's convenient for small projects, but I don't see how it's going to scale.
> It also makes it hard to edit the code as it's all in one big honking editor
> in RStudio.  Of course, I could edit the knitr source (format .Rmd for R markdown)
> in emacs and then knit it from the command line using a script.  There seem to
> be some robustness issues with editing while knitting, but I'm not sure that
> wasn't some other problem I fat fingered on the interface.
>
> Mixing text and code isn't so pretty.  I like my syntax highlighting and
> I like to be able to see all the code I'm I'm working on at once without scrolling
> around finding it interspersed with a textual exegesis.  I favor modularity over
> automatic gathering.  I also like using one tool for everything.  To pull our
> a cooking example, I'm a chef's knife and simple stainless steel pan kind of guy,
> not a gadget guy.
>
> I like managing all of my code separately and using my favorite editor to edit
> it and my favorite tools to run it, like make.  It's a pain to get started that
> way compared to just popping open a new markdown project in RStudio, but I think
> the up front time is more than made up by everything then being easier downstream.
>
> So I think I might like knitr better used outside of RStudio with
> more use of includes and less of writing into a single document.
> I had to write a little R script program just to dump unformatted code
> into the document. There's probably a more elegant way, but I couldn't
> find it.
>
> I do not at all like the code editor or the R Markdown editor in RStudio.
> I do appreciate the pop-up auto-complete and open global environment browser, given
> how much R programming idioms (and even packages) lean on the global environment.
> (And kudos to Jeffrey Arnold for getting that working in Stan's emacs mode, which
> I love!)
>
> I'm worried about applications of knitr to Stan because I couldn't figure out
> how to get knitr's make-like behavior to cache the Stan fit object so that it
> doesn't need to run each time.  Might it be because there's an outside file referenced
> in it?  I can't bring myself to write my Stan program as a string embedded
> in R code, but maybe that would work.
>
> After two days, I'm not sold on RStudio (but then I came in with a very
> anti-IDE prejudice).  As to RStudio:
>
>   * It's unstable and not only crashed, but crashed my
>     whole OS (I'm also not a huge fan of Mac OS X "Yosemite").
>
>     Maybe that's what Andrew's problem has been!  Avi Feller was saying
>     that RStan crashed in RStudio (not sure what hardware/OS), but never
>     when run from the command line under Linux on a cluster.
>
>   * RStudio gobbles some output, which I really don't like. Maybe
>     that's configurable?
>
>   * Like every other IDE, RStudio hides things and tries to be
>     clever by automatically foregrounding and backgrounding
>     windows and what not.  To change metaphors to the automotive
>     industry (I am from Detroit), I prefer to shift myself because
>     I haven't met an auto transmission that does it better (I hear
>     they exist now --- I'm a New Yorker now and don't own a car and
>     only rent crap cars like the Chevy Malibu I had in Arizona.)
>
> Also, what's with all these R package docs?  I found the knitr
> doc and web site, as it is, pretty much impenetrable.
>
>   http://yihui.name/knitr/
>
> In that way, it's just like ggplot2 (another RStudio gig), meaning
> that I had to go to third-person resources to figure it out.  Good thing
> there are so many great R tutorials out there!
>
> Markdown.  I really hate working in markdown.  This goes for
> WordPress, which uses WordPress markdown, and GitHub Wiki and issues,
> which use GitHub "flavored" markdown.  I'd rather just write the HTML since
> I'm going to have to figure out how it renders the HTML anyway
> if I want a reasonable output.
>
> The rendering of HTML and LaTeX is not seamless.  I wound up having to
> write a gazillion straight-up HTML elements and styles to do things like float and
> size pictures or to include captions.  That's an example of what I mean when I
> say these markdown languages make easy things easier and hard things harder.
>
> As a result, not everything shows up in LaTeX.   You can also write
> in pseudo-LaTeX and have things rendered to HTML with the opposite
> problem.  Or you can take a least-common denominator approach and get
> ill-formatted docs both ways, but at least they'll be the same.
>
> What's up with those awful knitr style sheets?  They violate standard
> rules of typesetting like making headers closer to the text they
> head than the text they follow.  Are there better ones somewhere
> someone could recommend?  I do like that you can drop in your own stylesheet.
> Then you just need to learn what knitr renders in the way of HTML
> (just kidding --- this is why I don't like "clever" tools getting in
> the way of my code;  if I wrote straight up HTML this issue goes away).
>
> I sent my completely knitted doc to Rob, and he couldn't render
> it on his machine.  Things seem to be messed up in both fonts and in
> content.  Maybe the former is due to missing a char encoding declaration.
> Odd, because it makes a 3MB web page that has everything inside it as data.
> You'd think they'd control the fonts.  Now why you get what look like stub
> captions when Rob renders it, I don't know.
>
> At some point in Arizona, someone (maybe David) mentioned that they liked
> that you don't have to paginate knitr output.  That does seem like a plus for
> code and its output.

> - Bob

In essence, the source for libstan.a was getting included and compiled by the interfaces.  The approach taken in the PR is the one described here http://stackoverflow.com/a/11709860/4294303 which truly makes it a header-only library and is a bit cleaner.  It relies on C++'s ability to ensure that a template is only instantiated once, regardless of how many translation units it is included in.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: U-turn using mass matrix?
messages.body_plain:
Here's a topic for the next meeting, or before:

I'd like to have another discussion about calculating the U-turn
condition using the (inverse) mass matrix.

I'm just thinking that if we have a 2D normal with zero covariance
but different scales, they won't mix equally because of the way the
U-turn condition is calculated.  By taking the inverse mass matrix as
a metric, we should be able to effectively renormalize.

Am I thinking about this wrong because we normally do only diagonal
mass estimation and the U-turn condition would suffer in that situation
if there actually was correlation?

Empirically, if I do this

fit <- stan(model_code="parameters { real y; real z; } model {y ~ normal(0,1); z ~ normal(0,1000); }")

I get

4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=1000; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=4000.

      mean se_mean     sd     2.5%     25%   50%    75%   97.5% n_eff Rhat
y     0.04    0.02   1.00    -1.93   -0.63  0.04   0.71    2.02  2487    1
z    36.21   19.36 982.97 -1830.71 -658.24 25.18 731.84 1958.58  2578    1
lp__ -0.98    0.03   0.96    -3.67   -1.37 -0.68  -0.30   -0.03  1071    1

wheras if I do this:

fit <- stan(model_code="parameters { real y; real z; } model {y ~ normal(0,10); z ~ normal(0,10); }")

I get very similar tail behavior and n_eff:

      mean se_mean    sd   2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y     0.18    0.21 10.07 -18.99 -6.60  0.03  6.95 19.57  2307    1
z     0.16    0.23 10.36 -20.74 -6.56  0.18  7.22 20.37  2015    1
lp__ -1.04    0.03  1.05  -3.94 -1.43 -0.73 -0.30 -0.03  1129    1

Adaptation is much much faster in the second case, but after warmup, sampling
times are roughly identical.

My intuition (clearly wrong in practice) is that the larger scaled parameter would
dominate the U-turn condition.  Does the dividing by the lengths cancel everything
out when doing the cosine?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] U-turn using mass matrix?
messages.body_plain:
Take a look at the right column on page 2 at http://arxiv.org/pdf/1304.1920.pdf.
The NUTS criterion is sensitive to the metric implicitly through the distance,
r = q_final - q_initial.  Anytime you contract position with momentum you’ll have
this sensitivity.  You can further see the effect of tuning the metric in Figure 2
and Figure 3 — a matching metric is better but in both cases NUTS is doing
the right thing.

I think what you’re seeing here actually has more to do with the leapfrog
integrator.  The first case is essentially a stiff system and until Stan can
learn how to correct for the stiffness trajectories will be slow (step size
decreases to the smallest lengthscale/highest frequency or you’ll reject
every proposal).  The second case is a non-stiff system that is initialized
in a  much better state and adaption is easy.

On Thursday, November 27, 2014 2:21:31 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>
> And we can deprecate the latter, though it'll be a bit of
> work changing everything, since the syntax is involved in almost
> every single model we've written or a user's written.

I don't see enough justification to get rid of the

y ~ foo();

syntax. It is similar to BUGS and similar to how a lot of models are expressed in papers.

> I think of the foo(y|theta) notation as an expression (specifically
> a function application) and thus evaluating to a value without
> side effects, so it may be confusing just using it as a bare statement
> that implicitly increments the total log density.

Maybe the syntax should have always been something like

lp__ += foo(y|theta);

but I don't see much point in having multiple equivalent syntaxes and don't see much point in breaking all existing Stan programs.

Ben

I completely agree.  One of the beautiful things about most stan models is that they can very closely mirror how a model is formally expressed in a paper or even when you're explaining something on the board.  Yes, it is somewhat overloading the idea of sampling or simulation, but if a user is struggling with the analogy of a model as specifying how data is generated then they (probably) don't understand what they're doing in the first place.

>
> > I think of the foo(y|theta) notation as an expression (specifically
> > a function application) and thus evaluating to a value without
> > side effects, so it may be confusing just using it as a bare statement
> > that implicitly increments the total log density.
>
> Maybe the syntax should have always been something like
>
> lp__ += foo(y|theta);
>
> but I don't see much point in having multiple equivalent syntaxes and don't see much point in breaking all existing Stan programs.

Breaking all existing Stan models seems like a heavy price to pay for a stylistic syntax change.  That said, we already have multiple equivalent syntaxes because we have y ~ foo(theta) and increment_log_prob(foo(y,theta)).

Yes, something like lp__ += ... more clearly explains what is happening under the hood, but we should also ask what differentiates Stan from a simple autodiff language like that used by ADMB http://www.admb-project.org/ whose models look a lot like Stan models, but without things like ~.  To me, a big differentiating factor is the natural connection between how statistical models are described on paper and how they are specified in Stan.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
I couldn’t quite tell from the paper:  is the idea that the program would find the transformations automatically, or that there would be some standard set of transformations that the user would use?  One thing that seems tricky is that the transformation would depend on the posterior density itself, right?  So, for example, if a particular aspect of the posterior density has a t-like shape, it would be appropriate to transform it based on the center and scale of the distribution, which in general the user would not know?  This would seem to suggest a two-stage procedure, where first the simulation is done with out any transformations (or, just using default transformations), then the center and scale and shape of the distribution are crudely estimated based on initial MCMC draws, then a scaling is chosen, and then MCMC is run again on the new scaling.  Is that what they have in mind for practical application?

I’m interested in these sorts of ideas (even though I can imagine Mike B’s reaction already!) because they could perhaps help with some of the unimodal approximation problems I’ve been thinking about in the context of wedge sampling.  So this does all seem worth discussing to me, even if the ideas could not directly snap into Stan.  (I also assume that this morphometric thing would work for HMC as well.  I was surprised to not see HMC mentioned in the paper at all, but maybe they’re saving it for a companion article.)

A

messages.body_plain:
Yes, I do think you would have to discover that your posterior distribution is not well-behaved and then go back and do it with the transformation. But their mcmc R package has a family of transformations given by the morph() function. I think the arguments to the morph() function could be specified as arguments to the sampler and then Stan could do the equivalent of morph() on the unconstrained parameters.

On my first partial read, I don't think random-walk Metropolis is too essential, since HMC also has difficulty with posterior distributions that have unfavorable tails and the transformation pulls the tails in. They were just able to show that you can get geometric ergodicity with the transformation and random-walk Metropolis.

Ben

On Friday, November 28, 2014 6:22:39 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> I couldn’t quite tell from the paper:  is the idea that the program would find the transformations automatically, or that there would be some standard set of transformations that the user would use?  One thing that seems tricky is that the transformation would depend on the posterior density itself, right?  So, for example, if a particular aspect of the posterior density has a t-like shape, it would be appropriate to transform it based on the center and scale of the distribution, which in general the user would not know?  This would seem to suggest a two-stage procedure, where first the simulation is done with out any transformations (or, just using default transformations), then the center and scale and shape of the distribution are crudely estimated based on initial MCMC draws, then a scaling is chosen, and then MCMC is run again on the new scaling.  Is that what they have in mind for practical application?
>
> I’m interested in these sorts of ideas (even though I can imagine Mike B’s reaction already!) because they could perhaps help with some of the unimodal approximation problems I’ve been thinking about in the context of wedge sampling.  So this does all seem worth discussing to me, even if the ideas could not directly snap into Stan.  (I also assume that this morphometric thing would work for HMC as well.  I was surprised to not see HMC mentioned in the paper at all, but maybe they’re saving it for a companion article.)
